extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners (biotechnology/chemical arts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. §112, first paragraph, with examples focused on antibodies, nucleic acids, process claims, and functionally claimed compounds. Aimed at determining whether the disclosure shows possession of the claimed subject matter across species, genera, and functional claim types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antibody disclosure must show possession in structural terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe an antibody in structural terms sufficient to show possession (e.g., deposit of a hybridoma or description of antibody structure in drawings or chemical formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of a deposit or structural description means the specification does not provide an actual reduction to practice of antibodies to other species; merely asserting binding activity is insufficient. (Applied in Example 13/14 where disclosure of murine antibody did not support claims to human/non-murine antibodies.)

rubrics_metrics.name: An adequate antigen description can support antibodies but only if antigen is described
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate description of an antigen may be accepted as sufficient to put an inventor in possession of antibodies against the antigen, but only when the antigen itself is adequately described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification does not provide a description of the antigen (e.g., human Protein X), then relying on antigen-description principles fails. See Example 13: antigen-based justification does not rescue claims when human Protein X is not described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure must provide correlation between species variants to support cross-species claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To support claims covering a protein (or antibodies thereto) from multiple species, the specification must disclose correlations (structural features or properties) between the disclosed species (e.g., murine) and other species (e.g., human or non-murine) that would allow recognition of other members of the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no correlation is shown and properties are unpredictable across species, disclosure of one species is insufficient to support a claim to a genus encompassing other species (Examples 14 and 15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional-only disclosure is insufficient without structural/physical/chemical detail
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure that describes an entity only functionally (e.g., 'human Protein X' by function) without providing its physical or chemical properties, structural features, or sequence does not satisfy written description for claims to that entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional identification without structural correlation leaves the claim directed to an unknown identified only by reference to another unknown; examiner should conclude failure of written description (Example 13 conclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method-of-making requirement when antigen/unavailable material is needed
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe a method of making the claimed antibody that can be performed without first having the target antigen (e.g., human Protein X) when the claim seeks antibodies to that antigen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the only disclosed method requires possession of the specific antigen, the applicant has not shown possession of antibodies to un-disclosed antigens (Examples 13/14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative number of species or common structural features required for genus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For genus claims (claims that encompass many species), the specification must either provide a representative number of species within the genus or disclose common structural features that distinguish the genus and allow identification of other members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single described species will only support a genus claim if it is representative of the genus by sharing common distinguishing features; otherwise the specification fails written description for the full scope of the genus (Example 15 and Claim 1 analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability in the art affects written description sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of predictability known in the art (e.g., genetic code predictability) can permit broader claims: where predictable correlations exist, disclosure of one form may allow those skilled in the art to envisage other structural embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: disclosure of an amino acid sequence (SEQ ID NO:2) plus knowledge of the genetic code allows one skilled in the art to envisage nucleic acid sequences encoding that protein, supporting written description for claims to nucleic acids encoding the protein (Examples 15, Claims 2–4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete sequence disclosure supports claims to nucleic acids encoding disclosed proteins
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing the full nucleic acid sequence (SEQ ID NO:1) and correlating it to the amino acid sequence (SEQ ID NO:2) supports possession of that sequence and predictable variants that encode the same protein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the specification includes a complete sequence and a method of isolating similar sequences, and the art provides predictable correlations (genetic code), the written description requirement is satisfied for claims to that sequence and to sequences encoding the disclosed protein (Examples 15 Claims 3–4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims supported when novelty resides in process steps and predictability is high
rubrics_metrics.description: If the novelty of a claim resides in specific process steps (e.g., complexing nucleic acid with a defined compound and specified incubation conditions) and practicing the process does not require unknown structural variants, the specification can satisfy written description for the method claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 16: disclosure of compound X, a working example (transformation of mitochondria in mouse cells), and predictable applicability to other nucleic acids/cells supports written description for a method claim even though component sequences are not all disclosed. Note: enablement issues are separate and should also be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening assay claims acceptable for methods but may not support product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosed screening method for identifying compounds (detailed steps) can satisfy written description for a method of identifying compounds, but does not by itself provide written description of the compounds identified by that method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 17: Claim 2 (screening method) satisfied written description because the steps are disclosed and are followable. Claim 3 (compound identified by the method) failed because no structural description of the compound was provided (reach-through claim problem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionally claimed compounds require structural or property disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that define compounds solely by their function (e.g., 'a compound that selectively inhibits POPKIN-2') require the specification to disclose complete structure, partial structures, or physical/chemical properties, or a correlation between target and inhibitor structure, to satisfy written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without such disclosure (no known selective inhibitors and no correlation), one skilled in the art cannot visualize the claimed compounds and written description fails (Example 17 Claim 1 and Claim 3 conclusions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic claim language ('comprising') broadens scope and raises representation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of open transitional language like 'comprising' yields genus claims that allow unspecified additional members; the specification must demonstrate possession of the genus across that broader scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should begin with narrower dependent claims (subgenera) to evaluate whether the broader genus claim is supported. If subgenera are described and representative, genus may be supported; otherwise genus fails (Examples 15 analysis of claims 1–5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual reduction to practice or deposit can support possession of species
rubrics_metrics.description: An actual reduction to practice (e.g., working example demonstrating the species) or deposit (e.g., hybridoma) provides strong support that the inventor possessed that species at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a working example shows the species (e.g., SEQ ID NO:1 cDNA or antibody produced), related subclaims directed to that species satisfy written description (Examples 15 Claim 4; antibody examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description and enablement are distinct inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Satisfaction of the written description requirement (showing possession) is a separate inquiry from enablement (whether the disclosure teaches how to make and use the full scope).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when written description is satisfied (e.g., Example 16 method claim), the specification may still raise enablement concerns that should be addressed separately during examination (practice note in Example 16).
